analysis.one_liner: Stops the IRS from collecting donors' names from tax-exempt groups' annual returns.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 240-182 on a near-party-line vote on June 14, 2016, but the Senate committee it went to never voted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the IRS from requiring any 501(c) organization — charities, social-welfare groups, unions, trade associations — to report the names and addresses of its contributors on annual tax returns, with narrow exceptions for the group's own officers, directors, and five highest-paid employees. Backers called it protection against IRS abuse of donor data. It passed the House almost entirely on Republican votes, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and received no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Donors to tax-exempt organizations gain anonymity from IRS review. That matters most for the large contributors behind politically active "dark money" groups — 501(c)(4) social-welfare organizations and 501(c)(6) trade associations that spend money on elections — since the agency that polices their tax status would no longer see who funds them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large donors to politically active nonprofits

how_it_helps.text: Bars the IRS from requiring the name, address, or other identifying information of any contributor to any 501(c) organization on annual returns, at any contribution amount.
Carves out narrow exceptions: disclosures tied to prohibited tax-shelter transactions, and contributions by the group's officers, directors, or five highest-compensated employees.

Backers' stated purpose is preventing IRS abuse of donor data; donor information filed with the IRS has in the past leaked, so donor privacy is a real, not hypothetical, concern for groups of all political stripes.
Supporters characterized the reporting requirement as a burden on associational and speech rights of donors, hence the 'free speech' framing of the title.

analysis.who_pays: The IRS and state charity regulators lose their main tool for seeing who funds tax-exempt groups, weakening enforcement against groups that abuse tax-exempt status or route political money through it. The public loses a channel of accountability for election-adjacent spending, since ordinary taxpayers effectively foot the bill for tax exemptions that would go unsupervised.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers every 501(c) organization, including groups that spend heavily on political campaigns, so the funders of election-influencing groups would be shielded from the agency charged with policing those groups' tax status.
The exceptions are narrow — only the group's own officers, directors, and five highest-paid employees must still be reported — so most outside funders, however large, would go unnamed.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost: protecting donor privacy for all comers also blinds regulators to exactly the funders most likely to be using a tax exemption for undisclosed political influence, and the bill offers no narrower alternative targeting proven IRS misconduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Donor privacy is a legitimate concern and the history of IRS data handling gives it weight. But this bill's remedy is a blanket ban across all 501(c) groups rather than a fix aimed at the abuse, so its practical effect is to remove oversight of political money flowing through tax-exempt vehicles. The privacy benefit for ordinary small donors is small; the oversight loss falls on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a party-line vote, went to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill 23-15 on April 28, 2016, and reported it to the House on June 9, 2016.

On June 14, 2016, a Democratic motion to recommit with instructions — an attempt to amend the bill's treatment of contributor identity for 501(c) organizations that take part in political campaigns — failed 180-238, with 176 of 188 Democrats voting for it and only 4 of 246 Republicans.
The House passed the bill 240-182 that same day: 239 of 246 Republicans in favor, 1 of 188 Democrats.
The Senate received the bill on June 15, 2016 and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which took no further action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the status quo held: the IRS and state charity regulators kept their access to contributor information, and tax-exempt groups that spend on politics did not gain the funder anonymity the bill would have given them. The large donors and politically active nonprofits that pushed the bill came out no better off.

for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage on June 14, 2016.

against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage on June 14, 2016, and nearly all voted for the motion to recommit.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 15, 2016 and never scheduled a vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, warning that barring the IRS from collecting contributor information would impede tax administration and enforcement.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost perfectly by party: on final passage 239 of 246 Republicans voted yes while 181 of 188 Democrats voted no; on the Democratic motion to recommit, 176 Democrats and 4 Republicans voted yes.

industries.industry: Politically active tax-exempt groups (501(c)(4) social-welfare groups and 501(c)(6) trade associations that spend on elections)
industries.note: The bill would let these groups keep their major funders invisible to the IRS, the agency that decides whether they keep their tax exemption. Their gain — an opaque channel for political spending — is the public's loss of accountability over election-adjacent money.

industries.industry: Wealthy individual donors to tax-exempt organizations
industries.note: Large contributors would no longer appear anywhere in filings the IRS reviews, gaining anonymity regardless of how the funded group spends the money. Small donors to ordinary charities get little benefit, since their gifts rarely matter to any filing in the first place.

Regulators would lose the contributor data they use to police abuse of tax-exempt status and to trace political spending routed through nonprofits. Their interest in keeping the data runs alongside the public's interest in knowing who funds influential tax-exempt groups.
